questions.questionText: What's the recommended order for trying to change an LLM's behavior, from cheapest to most expensive?
options: Fine-tuning, then RAG, then prompt engineering
Prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning
They're all equally expensive, order doesn't matter
RAG, then fine-tuning, then prompt engineering
questions.correctAnswer: Prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Each step up costs more in engineering complexity and iteration speed — prompting is testable in seconds, while fine-tuning requires a full training/eval pipeline and hours-to-days per iteration.

questions.questionText: Why is RAG usually the better tool than fine-tuning for adding new factual knowledge to a model's responses?
options: Fine-tuning cannot process factual information at all
Retrieval can be updated instantly by changing the document store, while fine-tuning doesn't reliably teach new facts and freezes again once training ends
RAG is always cheaper regardless of the task
Fine-tuning only works with images, not text
questions.correctAnswer: Retrieval can be updated instantly by changing the document store, while fine-tuning doesn't reliably teach new facts and freezes again once training ends
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning is better understood as adjusting behavior/style than reliably injecting new knowledge, and any fine-tuned-in facts are frozen the moment training stops — unlike a retrieval index, which updates instantly.

questions.questionText: What's a genuinely good use case for fine-tuning?
options: Any task you haven't tried prompting or RAG on yet
Extremely consistent output format/style at scale, where relying on few-shot examples in every prompt would be less reliable and cost repeated context budget
Fine-tuning has no genuinely good use cases
questions.correctAnswer: Extremely consistent output format/style at scale, where relying on few-shot examples in every prompt would be less reliable and cost repeated context budget
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning shines when you need very high reliability on a specific format/style across huge volumes, which can outperform relying on repeated few-shot examples in every single prompt.
